text: When Johnson came to write the Preface to his edition (Johnson 1765), he began from a principle that he held to be settled by long experience: "Nothing can please many, and please long, but just representations of general nature." That sentence accounts for the rank he gives Shakespeare among the dramatists of his age. The others, in Johnson's account, had drawn men as the customs of a particular court or city had shaped them. Their personages wore the habits and small affectations of a season, and spoke in the jests then current; when the season passed the figures passed with it, and a later audience was left puzzled or bored. Shakespeare drew from a larger and more lasting stock. His persons act and speak from passions and principles common to the whole race; their manners may be Roman or Danish or English, but the motive beneath the manner belongs to no one country. A reader a century and a half after the plays were written could therefore meet in them the father, the lover, the flatterer, and the friend he had already met in his own house and street, and could judge them true by that test.
